caseno: Appeal From Original Order No. 52 of 1992 with Civil Rule No. 58(fm) of 1992
lawyer:
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with SM CI Monir, Advocates ----- For the Appellant. 	 
MA Wahhab Miah with Biswajit Roy and B Chakroborty, Advocates ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Khalilur Rahman (Md) and others ------ Appellant
vs.
Abdur Rahman Bhuiyan alias Zinnat Ali Bhuiyan & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-3-92 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Chandpur in Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990 filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the case land. 

 2. The short fact leading to this appeal is that the respondent as petitioner filed the aforesaid case for pre-emption stating that his father Late Fazlul Huq Bhuiyan was the owner of the case land and the building and the petitioner-respondent lost his father during his minority and he inherited the case land and building along with other co-sharers. It is also the case of the petitioner that opposite parties 1-3 purchased 0.200 acre of land and three annas share of the building thereon from opposite parties 7 and 8 by registered kabala dated 22-3-79 at a consideration  of Taka 30,000.00. The present appellant further purchased 0.08 acre of land and one anna share of the building from Rokeya Begum, the predecessor of  opposite parties 12-20 by registered kabala dated  17-8-79 at a consideration of Taka 15,000.00. Opposite Party No. 1 purchased 0.0270 acre of land and four ann as ten gondas share of the building from opposite party Nos. 9, 10 and Rokeya Begum, the predecessor of opposite parties 12-23, by another registered kabala dated 7-4-79 at a consideration of Taka: 34,000.00 and opposite party No.3 purchased 0123 acre of land and 2 annas share of the building from opposite party No.l1 by a registered kabala dated 11-4-79 at a consideration of Taka 18,000.00. It is also the case of the petitioner that opposite party No.2 purchased .2070 acre of land and 4 annas 10 gandas share of the building from opposite parties 4, 5 and 6 by another registered kabala dated 14-4-79 at a consideration of Taka 34,000.00 and in this way opposite parties 1 and 2 purchased.0953 acre of land and 15 annas share of the building thereon from opposite parties 4-11 .and from Rokeya Begum, the predecessor of opposite parties 12-20, at a total consideration of Taka 1,31,000.00 but for these purchases no notice under section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was served upon the petitioner-respondent. It is also the case of the petitioner-respondent that he was minor when those kabalas were executed and registered and that he was ignorant about these at the time of transfers. It is also the case of the petitioner-respondent that his father died on 9-9-74 and the petitioner was the youngest son of his father who was born on 16-5-69, and he inherited .0310 acre of land and the share of the building thereon from his father and became a co-sharer in the building by inheritance. He came to know that his share to the extent of 0.0310 acre of land and the share of the building thereon have been transferred by false personation by two forged kabalas collusively and without consideration, which are void ab initio by alleged sale deeds dated 24-3-78 and 19-9- 78 and these were registered in the District Sub-Registrar's Office, Comilla for which Title Suit No. 117 of 1986 was instituted in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar Chandpur for a declaration that the alleged deeds are illegal, forged, collusive, without consideration and void. It is also the case of the petitioner that opposite parties 1-3 instituted CR Case Nos. 342 and 346 of 1984 before the Upazila Magistrate, Chandpur Sadar alleging that those deeds were executed and registered by the mother, brother, brother-in-law and sister of the  petitioner by false personation during the minority of   the vendor. It is the' further case of the   petitioner-respondent that he came to know about the deeds for which the present Miscellaneous Case was   filed from Salamatullah Khan and Habibur Rahman   for the first time on 10-5-90 and after getting the   certified copies of the deeds the petitioner deposited the   statutory amount of Taka 1,31,000.00 along with 5%  compensation and prayed for pre-emption under   section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 3. Before the trial Court appellant Alhaj Md Khalilur Rahman Miah and opposite party No., 2 Abdul Matin Miah entered appearance and contested the case by filing a written objections and their case  is that, the actual name Of the petitioner-respondent is Zinnat Ali and he was never named as Abdur Rahman and the deeds in question, for which the  pre-emption is sought for were executed and registered in the presence of the petitioner during his majority and the proceeding was not instituted  within time as prescribed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. The petition, is therefore, barred by limitation. The petitioner's entire share of the disputed land and building has been transferred by registered kabalas dated 24-3-78 and 19-9-78 and thereby his title to the case land has been extinguished and the petitioner is no longer a co-sharer in the holding. It has also been contended that this petitioner became major at the time of execution of the kabalas, which were done by him, in favour of opposite parties 1-3 and, as such, the I petitioner is not entitled to get an order of pre-emption. 

 6. Mr Khandker: Mahbubuddin Ahmed k appearing with Mr SM Moonir on behalf of the appellant, submits that the petitioner-respondent flied this miscellaneous case for pre-emption of five kabalas of different dates and when the petitioner-respondent sought to pre-empt the case land and building covered by these five kabalas heought to have filed separate case. He submits that the present case is a case of misjoinder of causes of action. He also submits that the five kabalas are not between the same parties and the dates are also different. Placing section 24(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that this section requires the filing of separate cases. There may be a joint trial but five separate cases ought to have been, filed. He submits that this section indicated that for each transfer a separate case is required to be filed. 

 7. As against this Mr M Wahhab Miah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner-respondent, placing section 24(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act submits that .this section clearly indicates that for several documents for pre-emption, one case may be filed and there is no bar in it and in support of his submission he placed reliance in the case of Hajee Majar Ullah Sowdagar vs. Mvi Nurul Haque & ors, 'reported in 23 DLR 68. It is submitted that in this decision a Division Bench of this Court found that one pre-emption case for different kabalas is maintainable. He also relied on another decision, which is of course a Single Benchdecision, reported in 42 DLR 253 (Sree Jitendra Nath Howladervs. Sree Bisweewar Howlader & ors) It is submitted that this decision has followed the principle 'of law enunciated in 23 DLR case. The learned Advocate contends that the facts leading to the decision reported in 23 DLR and the facts of the present case before us are similar though that decision was given in a proceeding filed under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 8. Before proceeding further with other arguments, we intend to dispose of the first objection that has been raised by Mr Khondker Mahbuddin Ahmed on misjoinder of causes of action. For proper appreciation of the whole matter let us look into the provision of section 24(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act."24(1) If a portion- or share of the Non-Agricultural land held by a non-agricultural tenant is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of such land may, within four months of the service of notice issued under section 23 and, in case no notice had been issued or served, then within four months from the date of knowledge  of such transfer;' apply to the Court for such  portion or share to be transferred to himself or to themselves, as the case may be." 

 9. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that the words portion or share is singular which indicate that there should be a separate case for each kabala. For proper appreciation of the whole matter let us look into the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act wherein it has been provided as follows: "96(1) If a portion or share of a holding of a raiyat is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding may, within four months of the service of the notice given under section 89, or, if no notice has been served under section '89, within four months of the date of the knowledge of the transfer, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves." 

 10. The language of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are same and similar. The learned Advocate failed to produce any decision of any higher Court on the point that in Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act cases separate applications for different transaction, are to be filed. So, we may profitably derive a sense of direction from the decision given under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 

 11. We have gone through the decision reported in 23 DLR 68 wherein one miscellaneous case was filed for pre-emption of three kabalas of three different dates. Parties to the case were also different In one kabala opposite party No. 1 of that case purchased from opposite party No.4 by kabala dated 18-8-66 and he also purchased from opposite party No.3 by another kabala dated 22-8-66 and opposite parties 1 and 2 jointly purchased from opposite party No.5 another portion of land by kabala dated 2-9-66. So, it appears that the vendors are different in these kabalas. In that decision the High Court Division observed that on a careful reading of the provision of section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it would be found that the transfer shall have to be pre-empted under certain conditions mentioned therein and in this case admittedly there were three independent transfers or sales. It is true that if by the document lands of several holdings are sold the pre-emptor can maintain one application for pre-empting the lands of all the holdings if his claim is not otherwise barred, but if the sales are different and independent then in that case the question is, whether the pre-emptor has to file separate applications for those independent sales or can he maintain one application for a number of independent sales. It has been held that the scheme of section 96 of the Act would show that the intention of the legislature is also not very clear on this point. The learned Judges after consideration of the relevant laws, including the Code Civil Procedure, ultimately came to the decision that an applicant under section 96 for pre-emption can join several causes of section against the defendants in one application arising out of several independent transfers or sales subject to the question of limitation and other conditions relating to maintainability of an application for pre-emption. 

 12. In the present case before us admittedly lands and building covered by five kabalas have been sought to be pre-empted in a single case. We have gone through the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and we find that as there is no clear decision from any higher Courts on section 21 of the said Act we may very well consider the principle of law set forth in the decision reported in 23 DLR 68 which was of course, a case under section 9p of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the language of both the sections are same and similar. Section 96 relates to a portion or share of holding of a raiyat, whereas section 24 is in respect of a portion or share of the non-agricultural  land held by a non-agricultural tenant. There is no difference in between the two sections. So, relying on the principle of law as set out in 23 DLR 68 and  42 DLR 253 we hold that the petitioner-respondent  can very well maintain the present miscellaneous  case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural  Tenancy Act even though lands and buildings of five  kabalas have been sought to be pre-empted in a  single pre-emption case and in that view of the  matter we find no force in the argument advanced by Me Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed in this respect So, on consideration of the submissions made by the learned Advocates of both the sides we hold that the present miscellaneous case is maintainable in law. 

 13. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed then submitted that under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act a co-sharer tenant of such land may, within four months of toe service of notice issued under section 23 and, in case no notice has been issued or served, within four month from the date of knowledge of such transfer, apply to the Court for such portion or share for pre-emption. He submits, that here in the present case the miscellaneous case does not come with in these two categories. It is submitted that the case was filed long after the period of limitation. 

 16. Now the question is whether the miscellaneous case has been filed within the stipulated time as provided under section 24 of the  Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. It provides that such cases are to be filed within four months from the date of service of notice or within four months from the date of the knowledge of such transfer. When admittedly no notice has been served upon the petitioner respondent he had to file the case within four months from the date of his knowledge. The kabalas are of the year 1979 and the case was filed on 15-5-1990. It is the definite case of the petitioner-respondent that in 1979 he was minor-and from the evidence en, record we hold that the petitioner-respondent has succeeded in proving that he was a minor in 1979 as he was born in 1969. From the perusal of the record it appears that the respondent earlier instituted a criminal case against the brothers and sisters of the petitioner alleging that knowing fully well that the petitioner-respondent is a minor they have defended him by creating a kabala showing this petitioner as major. This petition of complaint has been marked as Ext 3 before the trial Court wherein it has been categorically stated that the complainant on taking copy of the plaint and written statement of SCC Suit No.3 of 1984 came to know that this petitioner was minor when the kabala was executed and registered by showing him major. So this Ext.3 proved that on the date of filing of the criminal case, that is, on 23-4-84, the present petitioner-respondent was a minor. It is submitted by Me Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed that in this case the pre-emptor entered appearance and he had knowledge of the transfers but nothing has been• produced to show that the pre-emptor entered appearance and contested the case and there is no proof that the pre-emptor was aware of the kabalas. So, from this it cannot be found that the pre-emptor had knowledge of the kabalas from before 16-5-87. Even no evidence was led to prove that the respondent was aware of the kabalas in the later part of 1989 or in the earlier part of 1990 and within time he has not filed the case in question. The learned Advocate for the appellant placing the provision of section 8 of the Limitation Act submits that such pre-emption cases are not maintainable and barred by limitation. He further submits that as the case was filed beyond time the pre-emptor is not entitled to take advantage of the provisions of sections 6 and 7 of the Limitation Act Section 6 provides that where a person entitled to institute a suit or proceeding or make an application for the execution of a decree is, at the time from which the period of limitation is to be reckoned, a minor, or insane, or an idiot, he may institute the suit or proceeding or make the.  application' within the same period after the  disability has ceased, as would otherwise have been  allowed from the time prescribed thereof in the third column of the First Schedule or in section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 7 of this Act provides that where one or several persons jointly entitled to Institute a suit or proceeding or make an application for the execution of a decree is under any such disability, and a discharge can be given without   the concurrence of such person, time will run against all, but, where no such discharge can be given, time  will not run as against any of them until one of them becomes capable of giving such discharge  without the concurrence of the others or until the  disability has ceased. The learned Advocate contends that the advantage given to the litigant under sections 6 and 7 of the Limitation Act is not applicable to a pre-emptor in a case for pre-emption as provided under section 8 of the Limitation Act. He argued that as the pre-emptor-respondent cannot take advantage of sections 6 and 7 on the ground that he was a minor the present case is barred by limitation under section 8 of the Limitation Act. Section 8 of this Act provides that nothing in section 8 and 7 applies to suits to enforce rights of pre-emption, or shall be deemed to extend for more than three years from the cessation of the disability or the death of the person affected thereby, the period within which any suit must be instituted or application made. This section clearly indicates that within three years from the date of cessation of tile disability suit or proceeding must be instituted. This cannot be extended beyond the period of three years as provided' in sections 6 and 7 of the Limitation Act. Here in the present case before us the petitioner-pre-emptor-respondent attained majority on 16-5-87 and the miscellaneous case was filed on 15-5-90 which is admittedly within three years and it is in evidence that the petitioner-respondent came to know of the transfers from PW2 SalamatuIIah Khan and Habibur Rahman and thereafter he obtained the certified copies of kabalas from Comilla and filed miscellaneous case within four months as stipulated under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act So, on consideration of the materials on record and the relevant laws we find no force in the argument advanced by Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed on the point of limitation. 

 17. Admittedly, the pre-emptor-respondent is a co-sharer in the holding and from the evidence on record it is found that during his minority the lands were transferred in 1979 by five different kabalas without serving any notice upon him or upon his natural guardian and thereafter on getting the information the petitioner-respondent filed the present miscellaneous case for pre-emption within four months from the date of knowledge under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the miscellaneous case is not barred by limitation and in that view of the matter, we hold that the learned Subordinate Judge has not committed any wrong or illegality in allowing pre-emption and there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment
